entry.title: Digital payments fraud safeguards must come with banks' accountability
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Digital payments fraud safeguards must come with banks' accountabilityDigital payments fraud safeguards must come with banks' accountability

RBI's proposed safeguards give customers greater control over digital payments, but banks must remain accountable for preventing fraud and compensating victims

premium

The rapid adoption of digital payments has made financial transactions more seamless, but has also increased the risks of fraud

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 25 2026 | 10:23 PM ISTThe Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) recent draft amendment directions on preventive safeguards for electronic-banking transactions are an important step to prevent fraud-related losses. The proposals allow customers to set transaction limits, disable payment channels, and activate a “stop switch” to block future customer-initiated debits. The stop switch could be particularly useful when customers suspect that their accounts or devices have been compromised. It would block customer-initiated debits, new payment mandates, and registration of their accounts on new third-party Unified Payments Interface (UPI) applications, while allowing incoming credits. Certain existing recurring mandates and bank-initiated debits, including loan instalments and charges, would remain outside its scope. A trusted-person mechanism, which will be voluntary, will introduce an additional layer of authentication for high-value transfers.  The proposals build on a series of regulatory steps taken this year. In February, the RBI had said it would issue a discussion paper exploring calibrated safeguards in digital payments, such as lagged credits and additional authentication for specific classes of users like senior citizens. These ideas were set out in its April discussion paper. In June, amendments to the customer-liability framework for fraudulent electronic-banking transactions expanded protections, strengthened complaint resolution, and provided compensation for small-value frauds. The latest draft directions take this agenda further by giving customers greater control over how and to what extent digital-payment channels can be used.  The rapid adoption of digital payments has made financial transactions more seamless, but has also increased the risks of fraud. Digital arrests alone reportedly generated over 21,900 complaints, involving more than ₹647 crore, between January and August this year. Phishing, impersonation and coercion can manipulate customers into authorising transactions themselves, while money routed through mule accounts can disappear before complaints are processed. Customer controls alone cannot address all these vulnerabilities. Banks must invest in real-time detection of unusual transaction patterns, suspicious-account monitoring, rapid fund-freezing protocols, and effective coordination across banks, payment intermediaries, and law-enforcement agencies. The Supreme Court, while recently hearing a digital-arrest matter, pushed for banks to identify transactions inconsistent with customers’ past behaviour, temporarily suspend suspicious transfers, and compensate victims where failures in due diligence contribute to losses. This rightly shifts scrutiny towards banks rather than treating every fraud as customer negligence.  The RBI’s proposed expansion of the definition of “bank negligence” is, therefore, significant. It covers failures to implement authentication safeguards, issue mandatory transaction alerts, respond promptly to complaints, block channels after repeated failed authentication attempts, and implement customer-selected controls. System failures, security breaches, and employee or third-party collusion that facilitate fraud would also fall within the definition. Victims should not bear the financial consequences of institutional lapses. Grievance redress must be faster and more transparent, with clear timelines for investigating fraud, recovering funds, and deciding compensation. Banks must also ensure that the proposed safeguards can be activated quickly and easily. A secure digital-payment ecosystem cannot be built just by asking customers to be more vigilant. The proposals are a welcome step towards giving customers greater control, but the regulator must ensure that banks remain accountable for preventing fraud, responding swiftly when it occurs, and compensating victims when their own failures contribute to losses.     Topics : RBI digital payment UPI Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Nvidia saga exposes succession and governance risks for founder-led firms
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Nvidia saga exposes succession and governance risks for founder-led firmsNvidia saga exposes succession and governance risks for founder-led firms

Nvidia's leadership controversy highlights the risks of weak succession planning, political interference and excessive dependence on promoter CEOs

premium

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang | Image: Bloomberg

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 25 2026 | 10:17 PM ISTJensen Huang’s reinstatement as chief executive officer (CEO) of Nvidia has raised many questions about corporate governance and national security in the United States (US), and political interference in what should strictly be a corporate decision. The legal and reputational risks centre on Nvidia. However, the risks concerning national security and the US President Donald Trump’s involvement could lead to far wider consequences. The controversial decision by Nvidia’s board appears influenced by Mr Trump’s explicit desire to see Mr Huang back in charge. Mr Trump is reported to have a personal stake worth over $60 million in Nvidia. At the same time, the White House has blacklisted Megaspeed, the company founded by Alice Huang, the Chinese national with whom Mr Huang had a liaison. The lady is alleged to be a Chinese asset who may have wheedled secrets out of Mr Huang and enabled China to access high-end Nvidia chips.  Apart from security considerations, one of the concerns for investors is the lack of a succession plan. The world’s most valuable semiconductor manufacturer was (and remains) a one-man show, despite being a $4 trillion behemoth. Over 50 departments directly reported to Mr Huang. Since he didn’t believe in succession plans, his departure left Nvidia with a vacuum at the top. This concentration of responsibilities is usual in startups. But it is also the case in many tech companies that have moved quickly into the big league. The market valuations of SpaceX and Tesla, for example, are inextricably linked to Elon Musk’s personal actions. So is that of Meta, where Mark Zuckerberg has tight control of voting rights. Players in artificial intelligence (AI) such as OpenAI and Anthropic, valued in trillions, have similar issues, given that they are run by a few high-profile individuals.  In such cases, actions by the CEO (the actions that don’t directly impinge on operations) may lead to big swings in perceptions. However, as seen with Google, Microsoft and Apple, startups that grow at dizzying speed can also evolve to being run in a more conventional fashion, diluting the association of a company’s brand with an individual. Mr Huang’s return may seem to have kicked the succession issue down the road, but that’s not really true, given the overhang of national-security considerations and accusations that the President has interfered in the matter because of his interests. There was bipartisan condemnation of the reinstatement by the Republicans and Democrats. Mr Huang is scheduled to testify in front of Congress committees in January. By then, the Democrats will control both Houses of Congress and national-security considerations will be probed at length in those hearings. Many Republicans who are hardliners in their attitude to China may in this case be willing to go along with the Democrats. In that case, the reinstatement could have very far-reaching consequences.  The stock has seesawed as the saga played out. The retirement plans of many Americans are tied to Nvidia’s market value due to the structure of the US 401K retirement plan. Their net worth would have been significantly impacted by Mr Huang’s peccadillos. In India too, the emergence of an equity and mutual-fund culture has led to the net worth of many households being tied to market moves. The branding of many Indian companies is tightly linked in public perception to their promoter CEOs, and most also don’t have clear succession plans. India may see similar risks proliferating unless this event encourages corporations to consider setting such plans in place.     Topics : Nvidia Jensen Huang corporate governance CEO succession planning

entry.title: Nepal PM's India visit signals a thaw, but key demands remain unmet
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Nepal PM's India visit signals a thaw, but key demands remain unmetNepal PM's India visit signals a thaw, but key demands remain unmet

Balendra Shah's first state visit to India signals a thaw in bilateral ties, but differences over infrastructure, air connectivity and financial assistance remain.

premium

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's first state visit to India has opened the door to improving bilateral ties, with agreements on infrastructure, energy and trade, though differences over air connectivity and financial assistance persist. (Photo: PTI)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 11:44 PM ISTNepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s first state visit to India has offered an opportunity to reset relations, which have been unsettled for almost a decade. In choosing India, not China, for his first bilateral visit — unlike what his communist predecessor K P Oli did — Mr Shah signalled a willingness to overlook tensions to restore traditional ties. Significantly, China had extended an invitation to Mr Shah soon after he took office but preparations for a trip to Beijing were reportedly put on hold. The two-day visit offered New Delhi an opportunity to closely assess a leader who emerged from outside Nepal’s machine politics on the back of student protests and who has indicated a desire to be treated on an equal footing by his northern and southern neighbours with his “Nepal First” agenda.  The reorientation of relations was evident in the fact that both nations chose to set aside competing boundary claims, which flared up in May this year after Kathmandu objected to India using the disputed Lipulekh pass as a pilgrimage route to Kailash Mansarovar. Instead, Mr Shah and Prime Minister Narendra Modi underscored age-old civilisational links between the two Hindu-majority nations by virtually flagging off the Saryu-Kamala Express between Ayodhya and Janakpur, Nepal. Overall, however, the contours of the joint vision document, the eight bilateral agreements, and the development and infrastructure package suggest that India has chosen to be relatively conservative in meeting Nepal’s requirements. At the centre of the talks is India’s pledge of $1.6 billion for an economic and reconstruction assistance package following the devastating floods  caused by the collapse of a mountain glacier in August, killing about 1,500 people. The package includes a grant of $377 million for post-disaster and new infrastructure projects and a $1.24 billion line of credit for energy projects. The latter component reflects the damage caused by the floods, wiping out nearly 10 per cent of Nepal’s power-generation capacity, forcing it to turn to India to meet domestic demand. Given that Kathmandu has estimated rebuilding costs at $4.8 billion, there are indications that Nepal’s ruling regime would have preferred a larger commitment from India. Nepal, however, secured access to two ports — Kandla and Paradip — in addition to the existing rights at Kolkata, Haldia and Visakhapatnam — to conduct third-country trade, vital for a landlocked country.  An aviation agreement also partly fell short of Nepal’s expectations. Nepal has sought access to Indian airspace to attract international traffic to Bhairahawa and Pokhara, which serve as gateways to Lumbini (the Buddha’s birthplace) and the Himalayas, respectively. Both airports were built at high cost and incur heavy losses. But India has so far balked at permitting connectivity to these airports because they were built by Chinese state-owned contractors. New Delhi did, however, make bidirectional an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow, pending discussion over technical detail. Overall however, eight months into office, Mr Shah has made creditable gains with Nepal’s largest trading partner. Building on them will be his first big test in international relations.   Topics : Narendra Modi BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment India Nepal ties Nepal Power generation

entry.title: Fertiliser subsidy reform must go beyond sharing costs with states
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Fertiliser subsidy reform must go beyond sharing costs with statesFertiliser subsidy reform must go beyond sharing costs with states

Sharing the urea subsidy burden with states may ease Centre's finances, but pricing distortions, import dependence and inefficient nutrient use require deeper reforms.

premium

India's fertiliser subsidy regime faces mounting fiscal pressure, but shifting part of the urea subsidy burden to states may not resolve pricing distortions, import dependence and inefficient nutrient use.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 9:59 PM ISTThe Union government is considering converting the urea subsidy into a centrally sponsored scheme (CSS), requiring states to share the expenditure, as reported by this newspaper. This reflects the growing pressure on government finances from India’s fertiliser-subsidy regime. Discussion is reportedly still at an early stage, with possible cost-sharing arrangements of 70:30, 60:40 or even 50:50 between the Centre and the states. The rationale is to reduce the Centre’s fiscal burden while making states more accountable for fertiliser distribution and curbing diversion for non-agricultural use. However, transferring expenditure will not address the structural problems.  The fiscal pressure is considerable. The Centre had budgeted ₹1.71 trillion for fertiliser subsidies in 2026-27, but had spent around 86 per cent of it by November 16. Urea accounts for approximately 68 per cent of the budgeted subsidy. Expenditure on imported urea had reached ₹43,246 crore against a re-appropriated allocation of ₹44,001 crore. The Fertiliser Association of India (FAI) has estimated that the subsidy bill this financial year could rise to ₹2.5 trillion, 46 per cent above the budgeted amount. This is despite an expected decline in fertiliser consumption to 65 million-67 million tonnes from 70 million tonnes last year. The numbers underline that the subsidy burden is not simply a consequence of excessive consumption or diversion; global price volatility and import dependence are also important drivers. There is a case for greater state involvement in monitoring fertiliser distribution. States are better positioned to oversee local supply chains, identify unusual purchases, and prevent subsidised urea from reaching industrial users. However, there are limits to this argument. If the Centre continues to determine retail prices, subsidy rates, and procurement arrangements, the states will be forced to share expenditure without corresponding decision-making powers. It could also disproportionately burden fiscally weaker states, particularly those with large agricultural requirements.  More importantly, the proposed arrangement does little to correct the distortions in fertiliser pricing. Urea is sold at a fixed price of ₹267 for a 45-kg bag, with the Centre compensating manufacturers for the difference between the cost of production or import and the retail price. This makes nitrogen substantially cheap relative to phosphorus and potassium, encouraging excessive urea application and an imbalance in nutrient consumption. In this context, extending the nutrient-based subsidy (NBS) regime to urea deserves consideration. Under the NBS regime, subsidies are linked to individual nutrients rather than the cost of supplying a particular product. This could help rationalise relative nutrient prices and encourage balanced fertiliser use.  However, the transition needs careful calibration to prevent abrupt increases in farmers’ input costs. At the same time, cost sharing will not insulate public finances from international price shocks. India needs to strengthen domestic production, diversify import sources, and improve nutrient-use efficiency. Better monitoring through digital tracking and point-of-sale systems is equally important to curb diversion without creating another layer of administrative complexity. The fertiliser subsidy regime needs deeper reforms. Shifting part of the expenditure will not address the fundamental problems.   Topics : Centrally sponsored schemes BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Fertilizers fertiliser subsidy urea subsidy

entry.title: COP31 climate talks expose deep divides over fossil fuels and finance
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / COP31 climate talks expose deep divides over fossil fuels and financeCOP31 climate talks expose deep divides over fossil fuels and finance

COP31's failure to reach a political agreement exposes deep divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance, putting global climate goals further at risk

premium

A COP31 sign is displayed at the venue of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey. (Photo: Reuters)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 10:01 PM ISTNo one was surprised when the 31st Conference of Parties (COP31) summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended without a central political agreement — the Antalya Pacts — despite running into two days of overtime. If anything, the longest-running climate talks in United Nations history highlighted the festering divisions between the developed and developing worlds over fossil fuels and climate finance. The result is that it is now clear that global temperatures are set to overshoot the Paris-Agreement target of holding temperatures below 1.5 degrees centigrade above pre-industrial levels — at a time when global temperatures broke new heat records this year. The draft pact sought to call on countries to keep the overshoot as low and for as short-lived a period as possible, a considerable dilution from the original Paris-Agreement pledges, and suggested carbon-capture storage as a substitute for cutting emission. The latter in itself is controversial; it works for some industries but is limited as an economically scalable solution.  But it was fossil fuels that proved a key deal breaker — although the pledge to transition away from fossil fuels was taken at COP28 in Dubai three years ago. The draft pact excluded all references to coal, oil and natural gas or transitioning away from fossil fuels, replacing it with anodyne phrasing on the “irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development”. Refuting this framing was the European Union, the United Kingdom, Norway, small island-states and vulnerable states. This grouping was up against major oil- and gas-producing countries — most of them, not coincidentally, Turkish allies — as well as India, China, and Like Minded Developing Countries (LMDC). The other consequential point of disagreement was climate finance. A commitment to treble the figure by 2035 from $40 billion was articulated just last year. But the deepening North-South divide in climate talks means that the rich nations — the major historical contributors to global warming — were unwilling to commit to fixed contributions. At the same time, Russia accused developed nations of extending climate finance as loans rather than grants.  The 13 days of talks did record some gains, though the value of some of them is contestable. The proposed plan to raise electricity’s share in global consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 (the “35-by-35” deal) — which has morphed from a rigid mandate to a call for global cooperation — is one such. In countries such as China and India, for instance, the bulk of the electricity is generated through fossil fuels. At the same time, business deals worth $26 billion in agreements for renewables and grid pointed to some degree of momentum towards lowering greenhouse-gas emission. India’s low-key presence in Antalya reflected the shifting dynamics of climate talks. It continued to anchor its position in climate justice, Common But Differentiation Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities, equitable burden sharing, predictable finance for developing nation and an active opposition to climate-related trade barriers (such as Europe’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism). But it is notable that earlier this year, India withdrew its offer to host COP33 in 2028. As a result of the Antalya deadlock, many of the big issues will be carried over to COP32 in Addis Ababa next year.  Given the polarisation on the Turkish Riviera, consensus in a city on the edge of the Great Rift Valley looks just as unlikely.     Topics : Climate Change COP31 Global Warming Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: FPI disclosure rules need a wider review, not a response to outflows
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / FPI disclosure rules need a wider review, not a response to outflowsFPI disclosure rules need a wider review, not a response to outflows

FPI selling not only affected the equity markets but also put considerable pressure on the currency

premium

Representative Image for foreign portfolio investors (Photo: AdobeStock)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 9:48 PM ISTThe Indian stock markets have suffered considerably because of selling by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs). Although FPIs have made a strong comeback, buying stocks worth over $14 billion on a net basis so far in November, they remain net sellers to the tune of over $17 billion since the beginning of the year. FPIs had also taken out about $18.9 billion in 2025 from the Indian stock markets. FPI selling not only affected the equity markets but also put considerable pressure on the currency. There are various explanations for FPI selling and their recent return. Aside from global factors such as the war in West Asia pushing up energy prices considerably, and money flowing from across the world to companies in the artificial-intelligence (AI) business and related areas, it is also argued that taxes and regulatory requirements are affecting flows into Indian markets.  In this context, the securities market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi),  issued a consultation paper last week proposing the removal of the additional disclosure framework (ADF), which was introduced in 2023 for granular disclosures related to ultimate beneficial owners. The paper argues that many FPIs looking to invest in India see these disclosures as an additional compliance burden. Thus, instead of subjecting themselves to additional compliance, many investors may avoid investing in India. In effect, such requirements have become an entry barrier for FPIs. Under the current rules, if FPIs meet certain criteria on concentration or size, they have to submit granular details of all entities holding any ownership, economic interest, or exercising control in the FPIs up to the level of all natural persons without any threshold. Most jurisdictions don’t have such requirements.  The paper also highlights the stringent requirements under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, compared to other countries, though it is not in the regulator’s jurisdiction.  It is correct that in a world where capital is extremely mobile, it not only chases returns but also prefers markets where entry and exit are relatively easy. It is also reasonable to argue that India, which needs a sustained flow of foreign capital to supplement its domestic savings to achieve consistently high economic growth, should not be an outlier in terms of rules and regulations. In this regard, for example, a case is being made that capital gains made by FPIs should not be taxed in India as is the case in most parts of the world. It remains to be seen how this issue is settled. In the case of disclosures for FPIs, there is a need for a comprehensive review. Feedback on a consultation paper will not be enough simply because most stakeholders would not have full information. For instance, why was the additional disclosure framework introduced, what level of information has the regulator been collecting, and what has it done with that information? Similarly, why were the relevant provisions of the law against money laundering made more stringent in India than in other countries?  Therefore, what Sebi needs is an expert committee comprising officials from the regulator, law-enforcement agencies, and independent market experts. Such a committee will be in a position to examine all possible issues related to FPIs and present clear choices for both the regulator and government. Its report will also help inform public debate. Changes in rules and regulations should not be driven by the state of capital flows or prices on the ticker. They should be based on well-established and accepted principles.  This will also help provide stability and minimise changes.     Topics : SEBI Foreign Portfolio Investors FPIs Securities and Exchange Board of India Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: India's market rebound needs stronger growth to keep foreign investors
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's market rebound needs stronger growth to keep foreign investorsIndia's market rebound needs stronger growth to keep foreign investors

Foreign investors may be back, but India cannot afford to get distracted from the growth and reform agenda

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Akash Prakash7 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 10:07 PM ISTWhat a difference a month makes! From being ignored and at risk of irrelevance, India has come roaring back and how. In November, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have already pumped in $13 billion and the Indian markets are up about 15 per cent in dollar terms.  Given that Korea and Taiwan are down 15-20 per cent this month, we have seen a 3000-basis-point reversal in India’s underperformance in just 20 days. Breathtaking and also scary. The North Asian breakdown has been driven by the unwinding of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade, and is global in nature. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) is down 42 per cent from its 2026 high and 25 per cent in the last month. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are down 45 per cent and 55 per cent, respectively, from their highs. The Nasdaq 100 is down 20 per cent from its high and 15 per cent in the last month. The Neoclouds have got decimated, with Coreweave down 78 per cent. FPIs are now scrambling to cover their India underweights, given the brutality and speed of the rotation away from North Asia. We see large-cap stocks in India starting to outperform.  India has benefitted from the AI selloff, but is this change in mood sustainable, or are we going to get whipsawed, with foreigners dumping the country again as soon as the AI trade is back in fashion? This is really the question. Is the change in mood on India more structural or purely tactical? How to think about this?  India is unlikely to attract the value-investor crowd. The markets are too expensive and even after 24 months of weak performance have not become cheap enough to attract the value buyer. At 18 times earnings, it is hard to call India cheap. Domestic flows, their quantum and stability, now over $50 billion per annum and growing, do not allow the markets to correct enough to become truly cheap. This dynamic is unlikely to change until such time as domestic flows reverse, which does not seem likely anytime in the near future.  So we remain a growth market. Investors come to India to buy companies that grow strongly and consistently. This is the attraction. Growth investors only care about the pace of earnings growth, its predictability and stability.  Most investors believe that India can deliver on a sustained basis 15-20 per cent earnings growth. The logic being nominal gross domestic product (GDP) grows at 12-13 per cent, the listed/organised sector grows faster and with some increase in profit share/ GDP, we can underwrite 15-20 per cent earnings growth.  There was also the belief that we can deliver this for an extended period of time and with little volatility. This was quite unique in the emerging market (EM) world. Multiples ultimately depend on earnings growth, and the predictability and stability of this growth. In a world of 3-3.5  per cent real GDP growth, 15 per cent earnings stands out. For context, the S&P 500 has delivered earnings growth at a compound annual growth rate of 7 per cent over the last 50 years. Thus, we got the valuation and attention that we did. At its peak, India accounted for over 20 per cent of the MSCI EM index and was the second-most expensive market in the world after the United States. Growth investors were all in and we had limited competition in attracting flows.  What has changed post-ChatGPT is that we are now seen as a loser of the AI buildout. If our competitive advantage of having an army of trained white-collar workers is no longer critical, is there a risk to investor growth assumptions? With our perceived weakness in innovation and the lack of cutting-edge technology, can we keep up with the anticipated surge in global productivity?  What if global investors can no longer underwrite a sustained 12-13 per cent nominal GDP growth or a non-volatile 15-20 per cent earnings trajectory? If one were to question the secular case for Indian earnings, then why pay such high multiples? Lower and more volatile growth will attract lower multiples and undermine the investment case.  What has also changed is that with the surge in AI-related capital expenditure (over $1 trillion in 2026 alone), earnings across the AI ecosystem have got supercharged. In 2026, earnings growth in the US is over 30 per cent, let alone Korea/Taiwan, which are clocking over 50 per cent. Investors believe that these elevated capex levels will continue and, therefore, so can the earnings. Again, why pay 18-20 times for India, which is growing earnings at only 15 per cent, when one can buy the US at similar multiples and Korea or the EM index at 10-12 times earnings when they are growing much faster?  With supercharged earnings across the world, the relative attractiveness of India’s 15 per cent growth has dimmed. Growth investors chasing earnings now have a choice! No one seems to care that for Korea/Taiwan or the US these are peak-of-the-cycle earnings.  For context, memory companies are currently reporting operating margins of 75 per cent. Indian earnings, not being driven by an AI buildout are not peak-of-cycle and, therefore, should be less volatile. You should obviously pay less for peak-of-cycle and highly volatile earnings as they will inevitably revert to the mean at some stage. For investors, growth is both faster and cheaper elsewhere.  India is impacted by the AI trade on two fronts, the willingness to believe in the structural nature of our growth and earnings as well as the relative attractiveness of a 15 per cent earnings trajectory.  Thus, whether the move back into India is sustained or not depends both on what we can do as a country to reinforce confidence in the India growth story, and on whether investors continue to believe in the AI buildout, its sustainability and monetisation.  The more investors believe in the structural growth of India and its earnings trajectory, the more they will be willing to pay. We need to accelerate the reforms momentum. There is genuine concern among many on India hitting a middle-income trap.  The more questions arise around the AI infrastructure buildout and its monetisation, the more investors will start normalising the supercharged current earnings of AI beneficiaries. Then, 15 per cent earnings will start looking very attractive again. India may also benefit from being seen as a beneficiary of the diffusion of AI and the broadening of use cases. The AI narrative may move away from just focusing on the infrastructure buildout.  We need both to happen for India to continue to attract foreign flows beyond the short-term catchup trade currently underway. Strengthening the case for India is the only part in our hands. We should not use the current inflows to lose focus on the steps we need to take to improve growth and productivity in India. To attract FPI capital in a sustained fashion requires the hard work of improving India’s structural growth potential. Absent that, the flows may come to hide from the current tech bloodbath but will not stay.                
 The writer is with Amansa Capital     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Stock Market Foreign Portfolio Investors FPI inflows BS Opinion

entry.title: Ask businesses why they pass up export and investment opportunities
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Ask businesses why they pass up export and investment opportunitiesAsk businesses why they pass up export and investment opportunities

The government has been amending the guidelines and constituting committees to oversee implementation of the schemes

premium

Representative Picture

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 11:10 PM ISTIn February this year, the government unveiled several subsidy schemes under its Export Promotion Mission (EPM). Under some schemes, it appears, not enough exporters are coming forward to claim the subsidies. Last week, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade issued some trade notices relaxing the eligibility criteria, increasing airfare reimbursement rates and so on.  The EPM operates through two integrated sub-schemes, ‘Niryat Protsahan’, which facilitates access to trade finance, and ‘Niryat Disha’, which supports market access and addresses non-financial barriers to exports.  The six Niryat Disha interventions  are Market Access Support (MAS) to help organize/participate in trade fairs, exhibitions, buyer-seller meets and trade delegations, including airfare reimbursement for eligible participants; Trade Regulations, Accreditation and Compliance Enablement (TRACE) for partial reimbursement of eligible testing, inspection and certification costs to meet overseas requirements; Logistics Interventions for Freight and Transport (LIFT) for partial freight reimbursement for eligible micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in identified low export-intensity districts; Integrated Support for Trade Intelligence and Facilitation (INSIGHT) for supporting market intelligence, information on trade requirements and guidance to help firms identify and pursue export opportunities; Facilitating Logistics, Overseas Warehousing and Fulfilment (FLOW) for supporting access to overseas warehousing and order fulfilment infrastructure, including support for ecommerce exports; and the scheme for global outreach for branding, labelling and export packaging to help expand and sustain global markets for Indian goods and services by developing a unified brand India framework.  The government has been amending the guidelines and constituting committees to oversee implementation of the schemes.  Last Tuesday, the government enhanced the maximum eligible export turnover for availing airfare reimbursement under the MAS from ₹75 lakh in the preceding year to ₹50 crore, raised the airfare reimbursement limit up to 95 per cent for MSMEs and 80 per cent for other eligible entities, within monetary ceilings and reduced the mandatory membership period with export promotion councils from six to three months. Under the TRACE scheme, the government increased the number of testing, inspection, and certification entries eligible for reimbursement from 462 to 600.  Under the LIFT scheme, the government expanded the coverage of low export-intensity districts to 308 listed districts, expanded the categories of eligible gateways to include Land Customs Stations and Integrated Check Posts with an attached Container Freight Station, added inland waterways to the existing modes of transport, extended the air freight support for export shipments to Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, in addition to the North Eastern Region, reduced the minimum qualifying inland haul from 200 kilometre (km) to 100 km, with reimbursement limited to 400 km and extended the support to all exportable merchandise items, except those specified in the negative list of export products/categories.  It is too early to say how exporters will respond to these amendments, but one point is getting clear. The exporters will take the subsidies on offer if the activity itself, say air travel or participating in an exhibition, is justified on commercial considerations. A subsidy may tip the balance sometimes. Similarly, businesses may welcome the subsidies under the Production Linked Incentive and other schemes, income tax rate cuts, GST rate cuts, improved market access through trade agreements and so on but will invest only when it makes commercial sense.  The government should ask businesses which obstacles most often cause them to let go export or investment opportunities.

entry.title: The decade India turned the tide on poverty
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The decade India turned the tide on povertyThe decade India turned the tide on poverty

The next phase builds on this progress to lift the few people still at the bottom of the ladder out of poverty, while ensuring those who have already risen keep advancing and never slip back

Union Minister for Finance & Corporate Affairs Nirmala Sitharaman | Image: Bloomberg

Nirmala Sitharaman6 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 10:53 PM ISTA year ago, during my visit to Kiphire, an aspirational district in the remote hills of Nagaland, I interacted with tribal women from local self-help groups. Among them was Esther, a Lakhpati Didi, who proudly spoke of her millet-based products reaching customers online, far beyond Nagaland. What stayed with me was their confidence in a better future. I encouraged them to dream bigger and become Crorepati Didis. Their stories reflected a transformation reaching India's remotest corners, where geographical and economic challenges have long constrained opportunities, yet aspirations for a better tomorrow are growing. When the World Bank released its Poverty & Equity Brief on India last month, my interaction in Kiphire came back to me. The report showed that nearly 50 crore Indians had moved out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, while extreme poverty has been almost eradicated. These figures captured the transformation I had witnessed firsthand.  It was not always so. For over six decades after Independence, eradicating mass poverty remained an unfulfilled promise. Even in the early 2010s, India was portrayed abroad as a home of enduring destitution, lagging in sanitation, nutrition, clean cooking fuel and banking. The prevailing prescription was simply to put money into the hands of the poor, and poverty would take care of itself. The last decade has overturned that belief. Under PM Narendra Modi’s leadership, India has witnessed a fundamental shift from temporary relief to removing the barriers that perpetuate poverty. Guided by Antyodaya, the welfare of the last person in the line, our Government chose the harder path of addressing deprivations, household by household, ensuring development reached those who needed it most. Targeted, focused and tailored

'Kill switch': A new front in the global chip wars over tech sovereigntypremium

India can attract global capital if it removes barriers to investmentpremium

 Garibi is not merely a shortage of income or wages. A household without a secure roof, safe water, sanitation or healthcare remains vulnerable even when its income rises. One illness can wipe out savings and push a family back into poverty. Our government, therefore, made every intervention targeted at those who needed it, focused on measurable outcomes and tailored to the deprivation it was meant to remove. There was no magic wand. Each scheme required careful identification of beneficiaries, effective delivery and follow-up until the last household was reached. PM Modi has personally and painstakingly monitored implementation, intervened at critical junctures to resolve bottlenecks, ensured follow-ups and encouraged the use of technology to track delivery. This sustained attention has helped translate policy into tangible improvements in people’s lives. Health and dignity begin at home A family cannot climb out of poverty while illness and the daily burden of fetching water keep pulling it back. Under Swachh Bharat, access to household toilets has improved sanitation and helped avert an estimated 60,000-70,000 infant deaths a year. Jal Jeevan Mission has expanded rural tap-water connections from about 3 crore households in 2019 to nearly 16 crore, sparing women and girls the long walk for water and reducing exposure to waterborne diseases. Ujjwala Yojana has enabled cleaner, smokeless kitchens, while PM Awas Yojana has provided the security and dignity of pucca homes. Ayushman Bharat, offering cashless hospital care, has strengthened financial protection against medical expenses. Together, they act as insurance against the shocks that once pushed families back into poverty, while lowering household expenditure and freeing time for work. From a bank account to an enterprise Protection keeps families from slipping back into poverty; to rise further, they need opportunities to earn. For crores of people, that journey began with a bank account. Once, it was accepted that only fifteen paise of every rupee sent from the exchequer reached the intended citizen. Direct Benefit Transfer has changed that. Over 59 crore Jan Dhan accounts enable benefits to reach recipients directly, without middlemen. Technology has made this possible at an unprecedented scale. A bank account also provides a safe place for savings and helps establish a financial record, opening doors to formal credit. For those without property, access to the first loan can be life-changing. Two months ago, during an interaction with MUDRA beneficiaries, I met Sushmita Gharai from West Bengal. She lost her father during the pandemic, and her family’s printing business subsequently collapsed. With no land or gold as security, a collateral-free MUDRA loan helped her restart the press. Today, she employs 8 people, twice her initial workforce, and plans to expand into digital printing. What stayed with me was her determination to rebuild and grow. Her story reflects the aspirations of countless young Indians whose ambition exceeds their financial means. Under MUDRA, 60 crore loan accounts have been sanctioned, about two-thirds to women, while PM SVANidhi and PM Vishwakarma support street vendors and traditional artisans. Women have led this transformation. Ten crore rural women participate in SHGs that, through the DAY-NRLM and other programmes, have become platforms for savings, skills, credit and entrepreneurship. Over 3.7 crore women have become Lakhpati Didis, with some going further to become Crorepati Didis. Others, trained as Namo Drone Didis, now provide drone-spraying services to farmers. Women once excluded from economic opportunity are building enterprises and livelihoods of their own. The Sankalp for Viksit Bharat For generations, poverty was treated as something India could manage but never end. What appeared unimaginable a decade ago has now been achieved through years of steady work on the ground. Yet this is no time to rest; the road to Viksit Bharat by 2047 brings its own challenges. The next phase builds on this progress to lift the few people still at the bottom of the ladder out of poverty, while ensuring those who have already risen keep advancing and never slip back. The protection offered via various measures must now be complemented by even wider access to finance, markets and the digital economy. Government is building closer links between academia and industry through employment-linked incentives, internships and apprenticeships, while investment in infrastructure is connecting the country as never before. Opportunity cannot remain the preserve of a few.  The Prime Minister has said that Viksit Bharat, like freedom, is a commitment that every Indian must live. Having achieved in ten years what remained unfulfilled for six decades, India can face the next twenty with confidence. With the resolve of 140 crore Indians, Viksit Bharat by 2047 is within our reach, and we together will get there.

entry.title: Tax exemption for housing, but why not for MFs? A case for equal treatment
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Tax exemption for housing, but why not for MFs? A case for equal treatmentTax exemption for housing, but why not for MFs? A case for equal treatment

Tax exemptions favour NRIs and housing investments over resident investors in financial assets

premium

Harsh Roongta4 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 10:29 PM ISTDharam, a non-resident Indian (NRI), was discussing the revamping of his equity portfolio with me. He had been an NRI for decades and built up a substantial share portfolio by remitting money from overseas. He now wanted to sell and consolidate into an equity index fund. But the tax law put him in a piquant situation. If he sold his shares and bought other shares, the entire capital gain would be exempt under Section 115F of the Income Tax Act, 1961. But an equity mutual fund would attract full capital gains tax. “If attracting and retaining foreign currency into Indian equity shares was the motivation behind providing this exemption, then why are equity mutual funds not covered under this section?” he wondered. The law seemed to favour concentrated equity exposure and taxes diversification.  I remembered this conversation as I read that the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) had recommended concessions on long-term capital gains tax to the finance ministry. Sebi has reportedly asked for the long-term capital gains tax on foreign portfolio investors to be scrapped. It has also reportedly recommended that a switch from one mutual fund scheme to another should not be treated as a sale. A possible reading is that no tax would be charged when money moves from one equity mutual fund scheme to another after a year. This is like a gift or an inheritance. The receiver pays no tax on receipt. The giver’s cost and purchase date pass on to the receiver, who pays tax only on the final sale. The tax is postponed, not removed. The foreign investor may get an exemption. The resident investor may get only a postponement.  Back to Dharam’s question. I explained that the exemption was not discrimination against mutual funds. It was inserted in 1983 to help with the balance of payments situation. It allowed reinvestment in shares, debentures, deposits and government securities but not mutual funds. At that time, Unit Trust of India was the only mutu-al fund, and the industry was in its infancy.  Section 54EA, inserted in 1996, was a wider tax exemption. It covered all taxpayers and all long-term capital gains, if the sale consideration was invested in equity initial public offerings (IPOs) or mutual funds. The exemption was discontinued in 2000. One reason cited was that the low long-term capital gains tax rate left little justification for the exemption. Ironically, the same Budget widened the exemption for reinvesting capital gains in residential property. A taxpayer who already owned one house could now buy another and still claim it. The low-rate argument applied to all long-term gains. It was not applied to housing.  Twenty-four years later, the Union Budget of July 2024 broadly harmonised long-term capital gains tax rates, and the finance minister said every asset class has to be treated similarly. But neutrality needs more than uniform rates. It must extend to exemptions. Today the regime treats residents and mutual funds less favourably than NRIs and housing.  There are good reasons to encourage investment in housing and to attract foreign money into Indian markets. There are equally good reasons to encourage investment by residents in financial assets. How can the law exempt an entrepreneur who sells shares in his business to buy a second home, yet tax a retiree who sells equity shares to build a mutual fund portfolio for retirement income?  Truth be told, Dharam was luckier than that retiree. He found a workaround. He got the exemption and still diversified by investing in a portfolio of shares advised by a portfolio manager. Resident investors do not have even this tax advantage. Yet they are taken for granted, perhaps because they have nowhere else to go. Postponing tax on mutual fund switches is just a start. It is not enough. Residents reinvesting long-term capital gains in mutual funds or equity shares should get an exemption along the lines of the erstwhile Section 54EA with the same lock-in and cap that housing carries. After 26 years, it is time to reverse the decision made in 2000.

entry.title: Beyond the Jan Dhan passbook: Making financial inclusion more meaningful
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Beyond the Jan Dhan passbook: Making financial inclusion more meaningfulBeyond the Jan Dhan passbook: Making financial inclusion more meaningful

Banks deepen financial inclusion when they align earnings, livelihoods and risk protection through patient hand-holding

premium

ILLUSTRATION: Ajaya Kumar Mohanty

Tamal Bandyopadhyay8 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 10:00 PM ISTIn January 2025, South Andaman's official newsletter recorded a visit by senior administrators to a Jarawa settlement at Jirkatang to hand over voter identity cards to 19 members of the tribe, marking the Jarawa's first inclusion in the electoral roll. It was an electoral exercise, not a banking camp. Yet, it carries a lesson for every public institution: Service must move towards people, not wait for people to find it.  Another archival record, a presentation hosted by the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes, notes that insurance premiums were paid for 32 Onge individuals under the Janashree Bima Yojana from 2007, alongside livelihood support through the Onge Multi-Purpose Cooperative Society.  Such episodes capture what financial inclusion ought to mean: Recognition, access and protection tailored to how people actually live.  The finance ministry's Nationwide Financial Inclusion Saturation Campaign, running from 21 October to 31 December, gives India's banking system another chance to put that principle into practice. Steered by the Department of Financial Services (DFS), the drive covers 270,000 gram panchayats and urban local bodies across the country.  Going beyond account opening, camps run by banks, led by public sector lenders, are tackling a set of operational bottlenecks: Re-KYC (know your customer) for Jan Dhan and regular savings accounts, pending Central KYC identifiers, nomination updates for accounts and lockers, revival of inoperative accounts, and enrolment under the micro-insurance and pension schemes.  Former Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Y V Reddy coined the phrase "financial inclusion" while drafting the annual policy statement for 2006-07, released in April 2006, with Deputy Governor Usha Thorat. The term may have arrived in 2006, but Indian banking's push into the hinterland began in the late 1960s, with bank nationalisation and directed credit to neglected sectors and weaker sections. In the 1970s, the RBI laid down priority sector lending norms; experiments followed with regional rural banks, the self-help group–bank linkage programme and local area banks.  The current campaign is different in design. It is about fixing the plumbing of existing accounts.  In West Bengal, the State Level Bankers' Committee (SLBC) is working with member banks, district administrations, panchayats and municipalities, with a sharp focus on households from Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups.  In Punjab, SLBC convenor Punjab National Bank, peer lenders and district collectors are prioritising the revival of inoperative accounts across 13,236 village panchayats and 166 urban local bodies, backed by 7,669 bank branches and 98 financial literacy centres.  RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra on Saturday inaugurated a special financial inclusion camp at Vaksai in Maharashtra,  organised by Bank of Maharashtra. It focuses on re-KYC of bank accounts and expanding access to banking services.   Meanwhile, State Bank of India, which is the SLBC convenor in Assam and its neighbouring states, is steering the drive across Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura.  At the North-East Bankers' Conclave 3.0, held in Aizawl in October, the government reported that banks had opened 131 branches and installed 126 ATMs in the region between December 2024 and March 2026, and that 6,905 of 9,479 identified villages were now connected to either a bank branch or an India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) outlet. This progress predates the current drive. Of the remaining 2,574 villages, 2,515 will be linked through IPPB and 59 through brick-and-mortar branches.  The next phase of that expansion rests on a crucial regulatory tweak, announced at the same conclave. Elsewhere in India, the guideline for opening a brick-and-mortar branch requires a minimum population of 3,000. In the North-East, where difficult terrain and scattered hamlets make single-village thresholds unworkable, that norm has been lowered to 2,000 and applied on a cluster basis, allowing banks to pool adjacent villages to justify a central branch.  Yet bricks-and-mortar alone is not enough. Physical reach must be matched by explanations in the local language and reliable follow-up. The best camp is one where visitors walk away understanding both the service they received and their next step.  For communities such as the Jarawa and the Onge of the Andaman Islands, inclusion must also respect distinct social identities. Policy towards the Jarawa rightly emphasises protection from intrusive outside contact and the preservation of their social structure, subsistence and culture. In September 2025, the islands' cooperative newsletter noted that the Andaman and Nicobar State Cooperative Bank has 41 branches across 14 islands, while highlighting the role of Ellon Hinengo Ltd and the Tribal Development Cooperative Society in fostering tribal economic self-reliance.  On the ground, practical questions decide whether inclusion sticks. Who explains the form, corrects a clerical error and stays reachable after the camp packs up? Banks deepen inclusion only when they align earnings, livelihoods and risk protection through patient hand-holding, never through target-driven enrolment pressure.  Launched on 28 August 2014, the Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) remains the bedrock passbook of this effort. As of 4 November 2026, PMJDY had 597 million beneficiaries, 333 million of them women and 463.4 million banked at rural and semi-urban branches. Together they hold Rs3.28 trillion in deposits and 419 million RuPay cards. Public sector banks carry the bulk of the load with 459 million accounts, while regional rural banks hold another 112 million.  Now consider how the camp priorities are trying to make those accounts work harder.  To ease re-KYC friction, the RBI in June 2025 allowed banks to use authorised business correspondents to collect self-declarations from customers whose KYC details are unchanged or where only the address has changed, subject to safeguards, while keeping the bank accountable for completing the update.  For dormant money, the RBI's UDGAM (Unclaimed Deposits – Gateway to Access inforMation) portal lets citizens search for unclaimed balances across banks in one place. Deposits left unclaimed for 10 years move to the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund, yet depositors or their legal heirs can claim them at any time, with no time limit.  Social security forms the next pillar. The Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) offers life cover of Rs 2 lakh for death from any cause at an annual premium of Rs 436. Open to account holders aged 18 to 50 and renewable up to the age of 55, it is a pure term cover with no maturity value, and new or rejoining subscribers face a 30-day waiting period for deaths other than by accident. By 22 July 2026, cumulative enrolments stood at 280.6 million with over 1 million claims settled up to 30 June 2026.  Along with it, the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY) gives account holders aged 18 to 70 a cover of Rs 2 lakh for accidental death or permanent total disability (and Rs 1 lakh for permanent partial disability) for Rs 20 a year. Cumulative enrolments reached 591 million by 22 July 2026, with 189,057 claims disbursed up to 30 June 2026. Crucially, PMSBY is an accident cover, not a health policy; it does not reimburse hospital bills.  Both schemes rely on consent-based auto-debit and annual renewal. Consent matters because a family that knows a policy exists is far more likely to file a timely claim. Rather than touting cumulative enrolments alone, banks and insurers should publish the number of active policies, renewal success rates and lapses. Debiting a premium from a Jan Dhan account does not automatically translate into effective protection.  Can a bereaved family identify the insurer, recognise the premium debit in a passbook and navigate the claim paperwork? Banks' duty of care must extend to renewal alerts, minimum-balance reminders, help with documentation and claim channels that people can understand.  Similarly, the Atal Pension Yojana (APY) guarantees a minimum monthly pension of between Rs 1,000 and Rs 5,000 after the age of 60 to citizens who join between the ages of 18 and 40, do not pay income tax and contribute regularly until retirement. As of 8 November 2026, APY had 81 million active subscribers and Rs 60,299 crore in assets under management. Because APY is a long-term contributory commitment, not a free dole, bankers must explain contribution obligations and exit rules clearly before signing anyone up.  The Jarawa electoral roll was an act of civic recognition, not an insurance drive. But its lesson for banking is unmistakable: Institutions earn trust when they listen, return and see the job through, turning financial inclusion from a form-filling exercise into an enduring relationship.  _____________________________________________________________________________________________________ The writer is an author and senior advisor to Jana Small Finance Bank Ltd.
